title: Reformation Day (31 October)
hook: Lutherans and others remember 1517, now often with Catholic neighbors

segments.voice: Yesterday, Teresa's day, and a slip of paper in a prayer book. Your line was god alone suffices. Did you reach for the bookmark? Day one thousand fifty-four.

What does it take for a church to say, out loud, we need fixing? On the last day of October, while some streets fill with costumes and pumpkins, Lutheran churches and others keep a quieter anniversary. Tradition says that on the eve of All Saints, a friar and teacher named Martin Luther posted a set of theses, points for debate, on the church door in Wittenberg, in Germany, questioning the sale of indulgences, which Catholic teaching describes as release from punishment still due for sins already forgiven. What followed split Western Christianity. And in recent years, in some places, Lutherans and Catholics have begun marking the day side by side. Today, Reformation Day.

For Luther, much turned on a verse. In Paul's letter to the Romans, in the King James Bible: "The just shall live by faith." Luther came to read it as good news: that God makes people right as a gift, received by trust, not bought or earned. Ephesians puts it plainly: "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God." So when he saw indulgences being sold, he objected. The argument grew far beyond what one set of theses could hold. Churches divided. The years that followed were bitter, and in places bloody, on more than one side. That history is part of the day, and it's honest to say so. Then the carry. Semper reformanda, a Latin motto later taken up in Reformed churches. In full it's often given as: the church reformed, and always being reformed. The point is that reform is not a single event in the past. On this view, a church that thinks it has finished reforming has stopped listening. Paul's line in Romans fits it: "be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind." Some readers hear that as ongoing, not once. Catholics have their own way of saying this. The Second Vatican Council spoke of Christ calling the church to continual reformation, as it goes on its pilgrim way. Lutherans and Catholics have since signed a joint statement on how God makes sinners right, and some now pray together on this day, with thanks for what each has received, and sorrow for the wounds of division. Different churches, still different in real ways. But on one point they can say the same words: always being reformed.

Here's the practice: pray for your own church's reform. Not someone else's. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a community you belong to: a church, if you have one, or a family, a team, a workplace. Name one thing in it that needs mending. Keep it specific, and keep it close to home. Then name one part you play in it, however small. If you pray, you can ask God to reform your church, beginning with you. If you don't, just hold that one thing, and your part in it, honestly, without blame. The bell holds the time.
Reformation Day. The day Lutherans and others remember Martin Luther's theses and the reform that followed, kept now, in some places, alongside Catholic neighbors.
Your line: semper reformanda. Always being reformed. Today, fix one small thing in a place you belong, without waiting for anyone else to go first. Day one thousand fifty-four.

howItsDone: Lutheran and some other Protestant churches keep Reformation Day at the end of October with hymns and readings on grace and faith, and in some places Lutherans and Catholics now hold joint services of prayer.

notes: Claims rule: no year (1517) and no number of theses are spoken; the posting is framed as 'tradition says'. The index hook field still contains 1517 as written by the outline.

'What followed split Western Christianity' and 'the years that followed were bitter, and in places bloody, on more than one side' are historical summaries; confirm fair to Lutheran and Catholic readers.
Semper reformanda: 'a Latin motto later taken up in Reformed churches' and the fuller form 'the church reformed, always being reformed'; please check attribution.
Vatican II paraphrase (Unitatis Redintegratio 6, 'continual reformation') and the Lutheran–Catholic joint statement on justification; confirm wording, no dates given.
Luther's reading of Romans is described as his reading; the script does not say who was right.

Editor pass: replaced 'forgiveness being sold' (unfair to Catholic teaching, which distinguishes indulgences from forgiveness) with the sale of indulgences in hook, teach and myth; softened 'Luther's trouble began with a verse'; attributed 'a church that thinks it has finished...' to the motto's view; turned 'Not once. Ongoing.' into a reading.

Audit pass (fresh auditor, 2026-10-01): 'church pardons tied to the teaching on sin' blurred Catholic teaching (indulgences concern punishment due for sins already forgiven, not forgiveness itself); now stated as Catholic teaching describes it. Luther was an Augustinian friar, so 'monk' became 'friar'. Keeper: confirm both.
